blocks.text: Today in Tedium: Last week, my past caught up with me. In 2026, I found myself looking at every embarrassing thing I ever posted on Usenet—bad song lyrics, jokes I thought were clever but got zero replies, an argument with someone about Taco Bell, even my attempt at a makeshift pop chart. It was an unusual feeling, not unlike the feeling you might have of looking at an old book of poetry you wrote before you really had an idea of what you were doing. I feel like Olivia Rodrigo, watching her old grade-school talent show videos go viral after she became better known for videos like this one. (This is the only way I feel like Olivia Rodrigo.) A recent tool has gotten me thinking about Usenet once again—and what it means for conversations that died decades ago to resurface far from their original context. Today’s Tedium considers looking at a Usenet archive, 30 years later. — Ernie @ Tedium

The year Google stopped adding new posts from Usenet into Google Groups. (The old ones are technically still online, but it’s clear the platform isn’t particularly well maintained. I think that team is working on ensuring that a Gemini sparkle is in every Google app.) By that time, many newsgroups had been overrun by spam, so in a sense, it was probably time. But it’s always been a tough racket to actually read the Usenet archive on Google Groups, despite the fact that it was based on an archive built by DejaNews, which offered one of the first real Usenet archival efforts.
Millions of old posts, no binaries: The data nerd who made a giant vintage database searchable

This ain’t our first Usenet rodeo. Far from it. Tedium’s talked about it a lot, actualy. Back in 2017, we reported on the disruptive role that binary file-sharing played in Usenet’s evolution. (It’s weird how little we thought about things like security and safety in the early ’90s.)

The year prior, I highlighted the tale of Usenet charthound Matt Levine. And in 2019, we published an article describing how modern day Trump whisperer Michael Wolff leveraged Usenet spam to build his early journalistic reputation.
And then there’s this 2020 post on the Eternal September, a Usenet-borne phenomenon that I think holds up pretty well, all things considered.

But the thing about these stories is that I always ran into a problem when trying to resurface the thing I was talking about. Too often, I would land on third-hand websites or have to dig incredibly hard to find a suitable result on Google Groups, the platform that was supposed to archive this content.

At some point, Google unnecessarily neutered its archive. Yes, many of the messages were still there, but it seems like the company intentionally made it difficult to search through the engine, only offering the most basic sorting abilities. Which means that, if you’re trying to (for example) figure out when the term “Eternal September” was first expressed on Usenet, you would not be able to find it without a lot of extra work. (In fact, the only way to figure it out might be by referring to a Google Groups link on Wikipedia—a link that, as of this writing, gives me a 429 error.)

Usenet-Rewind, a new service by the firm Erie Data Systems, makes it far easier to narrow in on an incredibly complex archive. I asked it to conduct that same search for the phrase “Eternal September,” oldest date first, and the very first result, the very post by John William Chambless referenced in the Wikipedia article, showed up like it was nothing.
That’s despite the fact that the archive has more than a billion messages in it—or, to be exact, 1,039,260,173 messages as of this writing—dating to 1981.
More searching of stuff I researched a while ago: An early post from chartster Matt Levine, promoting his mailing list on rec.music.misc, appeared on September 5, 1995:

Subscribe to the coolest new mailing list, Matt Levine’s Top 40. THe main chart is based on my opinion. There is also a cool chart where you get to vote for your favorite songs called Netizens’ Picks. If you would like to subscribe, e-mail me at [address redacted].-matt levine

Michael Wolff’s attempts to draw attention to his Net Guide offerings started showing up in the early weeks of 1994, first in alt.online-service and numerous other newsgroups, complete with quotes from Electronic Frontier Foundation founder John Perry Barlow and early Wired editor Louis Rossetto. The drama around his company’s posts getting mass-cancelled for spamming, which hit at the end of 1994, is shared in its entirety.

As for the binaries that reshaped Usenet? Curiously, I don’t see any groups under alt.binaries, though I see a number of groups with misspellings of the word binaries. I did find some groups that specialized in software downloads, such as alt.ibm.warez, and I spotted a note that specifically states “<uuencoded_portion_removed>.” I guess what I’m saying is that you should not expect to download 35-year-old warez from Usenet-Rewind.
But that’s fine. Because honestly what’s there is pretty impressive.

So, how come this new thing has a significantly better search experience than even what Google has on offer? And how come nothing else has even gotten close? Perhaps it comes down to right time, right person. Erie Data Systems founder Craig J. Stadler says that he got into Usenet in his early 20s, but and he felt the same limitations with Usenet research that I did.

“Every resource I found wasn’t even close to what I wanted in regards to research,” he says. Unlike me, he could do something about it, as he has spent the past decade and a half working on search engine architecture using Apache Solr, a high-speed open-source search platform.

“I made it my mission to make this,” he says. Stadler is a big-data guy who has built massive databases in the past, but even by that standard, Usenet is a particularly large corpus. He apparently spent a full year acquiring data for Usenet-Rewind though a number of resources in what he calls a “no-stone-unturned” approach.
“Many, many archives and resources of dumps, backups, and donations were involved,” he says. “I also built an NNTP Usenet crawler to fill in the gaps and get all new public Usenet data.”

(This was how I learned that there’s a niche RSS reader tool out there that has been archiving every issue of Tedium on Usenet for the past seven or eight years, which, nice work. At least someone’s using Usenet exactly as it was originally intended.)

The result is one of the most in-depth Usenet archives I’ve seen online, bringing a kind of modern searchability to a service that is traditionally the domain of dedicated clients that haven’t gotten significant upgrades in years. (Plus, it makes room for the casual user. It is possible to use it for free for a limited number of searches with a new account, though if you’re using it with any seriousness, you’ll likely want to pay for a $9.99/month plan.)
As someone who digs through stuff like patent filings and old newspaper articles, it has always been kind of a disappointing gap that we’ve never had a real Usenet archive online.
This fills it. But it does cut both ways.
“You should know that Usenet, the battleground for what has become known as The War Between alt.tasteless and rec.pets.cats, is the Internet’s answer to Time Warner’s 500 channels of cable.”
— A May 1994 assessment of Usenet, according to an article in Wired discussing an epic flame war between two stylistically divergent newsgroups. Truer words have never been written.
The weird feeling that stewing in 30-year-old Usenet posts gives you

That Olivia Rodrigo example from earlier is not really a one-off. Much the opposite. It’s the kind of experience many people under the age of 35 are basically used to at this point: An internet in which their youthful memories and embarrassing moments are just a click away.

The college student who saved all of their old drinking photos on Facebook or Flickr, the person with the embarrassing Tumblr blog? It’s all still online, waiting for someone to find it. Our collective digital memory has not been particularly well-curated.

But Usenet was like a big redo for a number of large groups of people, because for decades, the archive was frustratingly incomplete and otherwise hard to reach. Yes, some of it seeped out, but digging for an old Usenet post, even if you remembered your old email address, felt like an archaeological dig.

I think what stands out to me about Usenet-Rewind is that it more or less captures all of it, warts and all. I did a search for my late ’90s email address, and found numerous entries under my name. I then did a search at my email addresses for the two colleges I went to and found a bunch more posts. And I’m not going to lie, most of those posts were not written with the assumption that they would be a part of the permanent record 25 years later.

So I had my version of the Olivia Rodrigo talent show thing, with a shaky voice and slightly unsure footing, except my voice was completely digital. I was still figuring out what I wanted to put out there, so I put everything out there. Penpal requests. Song lyrics. Attempts to extract advice on my budding career. Attempts to figure out chords for songs when I barely knew how to play guitar. My own personal rock chart, inspired by Matt Levine’s.
And all of that stuff resurfaced, rushing back and reminding me that, oh yeah, you barely knew what you were doing on the internet at this time. I’m sure I’m far from alone on this front.

Which naturally leads to some privacy questions. Do you want a service resurfacing things that you wrote 30 years ago, presuming that the content would eventually disappear from the face of the internet after a month? (Perhaps this is the reason why Google intentionally weakened the search on Google Groups? Notably, Google was once sued over Usenet posts on Google Groups, but won the case in a federal appeals court.)

For Stadler’s part, he points to the fact that he offers the ability to do DMCA takedown notices. So if Michael Wolff decided that he didn’t want people to check out his ’90s attempts at spam, he presumably could send one to Usenet-Rewind and they would take it down. (That said, a DMCA request does have some limits: “Removal from our index does not delete the content from Usenet itself,” the page states.)

But what about LLMs, which have made Reddit posts into one of their most valuable information sources over the past few years? Stadler makes clear that this data was not gathered for this purpose. “To our knowledge this data is not legally OK to use in an LLM, and we have no intention of going beyond traditional tokenized search,” he says.

That said, if you did want to look at Usenet in a programmatic way, perhaps to do sentiment analysis of different groups or academic research, the firm does offer a higher-tier plan which includes API access, allowing for deeper, more specific searches of the archives (within reasonable limits). But at $39.99 per month, you’re paying for the privilege.

The fact of the matter is, this is a corpus that goes back decades, is extremely complete, and taking old posts down might be like a game of Whack-A-Mole. Put another way: Your vintage standards of privacy don’t match your modern ones, and that means your awkward moments, your fights over Star Trek plots, your bad takes on The Simpsons, will remain on someone’s Usenet server forever.
Over the years I’ve spoken passionately about the need to keep old content alive online, to discourage companies from taking it down based on whatever whim they’re feeling on a given day.

Usenet, while never fully taken offline, has never quite been as accessible as it once was. For better or worse, Usenet-Rewind solves that in ways that other tools like UsenetArchives.com have never quite been able to. For one thing, the search actually works! (Some will point out that GigaNews also has in-depth archives, which I’ll concede, but that’s not quite built for casual users to dive into.)

The fact is, Usenet hasn’t been a truly mainstream experience for a long time. (Mozila Thunderbird, not exactly the world’s most popular email client, is the closest thing we have to a news reader that folks have heard of.) But it’s packed with information, much of it extremely niche, some of it super-useful. From a research standpoint, being able to dive into this information the way I might on Newspapers.com or Google Patents is a really exciting prospect.

Here’s an example: Back in the mid-1990s, MTV would frequently hold moderated online chats with celebrity figures on AOL and, later, IRC. (I mentioned one such chat, with the Butthole Surfers, way back in 2017.) These chats were all but forgotten after that moment, but many of the transcripts for these ended up on Usenet. A few I found after a couple minutes of digging:
Iggy Pop (in response to a question about whether he gets stage fright): “don’t get so personal,creepo.”
Mike Judge (in response to a question asking if he’s real): “If you had put a question mark at the end of that sentence I might have been able to answer”
Chris O’Donnell (in response to a question about what it was like to play a soldier in a war movie): “The fake blood was kinda sticky but it was better than a real bullet in your leg.”

Marilyn Manson (in an introduction ahead of an IRC chat): “I think people should have a better attitude towards the newer Marilyn Manson fans because it’s just one more step towards bringing or ideas into the mainstream and I’d rather see them being ‘Marilyn Manson poseurs’ than listening to Hootie & The Blowfish.”

John Popper (when asked for his views on Kraft Macaroni & Cheese): “I believe that a scam is being perpetrated on the American people. they set up a cute innocent young looking girl to say that there’s so much cheese involved but the cheese should precede the macaroni. But on my own investigation I have found only hollow macaroni spray painted lightly with a cheese-like sauce. I would call it Kraft lightly spray painted with a cheese-like sauce macaroni. Besides, Stouffers kicks butt”

This information required someone to care enough to copy and paste it elsewhere. It might have been forgotten otherwise. And Usenet-Rewind is full of stuff like this. It’s a treasure trove, and in the right hands, it could lead to some truly fascinating discoveries. After all, when it comes to history, ephemera is often more effective at getting an on-the-ground assessment of a culture than high-level nostalgia.

Usenet can be best thought of as a network of ephemera, and it helps fill the gaps of the pre-Web era that the Internet Archive has rarely been able to capture. (Something tells me that opposition researchers are going to love this thing, because odds are at least some modern-day politicians posted on Usenet in the ’90s.)
Can a thing be an important resource and a potential privacy violation? It’s an open question. But I’m just happy that vintage Usenet is a little easier to access these days.

Thanks to Craig J. Stadler of Erie Data Systems for taking the time to chat about this interesting thing he made. Give Usenet-Rewind a look! You might even find yourself hiding in one of these old newsgroups.
Find this one an interesting read? Share it with a pal!
And if you love old digital culture, our sponsor Computer Chronicles Revisited is very much gonna be up your alley.

Can a thing be an important resource and a potential privacy violation? It’s an open question. But I’m just happy that vintage Usenet is a little easier to access these days.

blocks.text:
Since people keep asking how this blog is made, and I don’t want to share the
awful, terrible code that it is taped together with, I’ve decided to start
explaining parts of it piecewise. Generally, any time something breaks and I
have to fix it, I write down what I did and what it connects to.

The most recent issue was the stack limit being blown by a helper function
involved in generating the tag index. I had written it to be explicitly
recursive, which worked fine with a small-ish number of published articles, but
not anymore. The tag index creation follows a similar pattern to the rss feed
generation detailed in the previous article.

(defun tw-tag-index (project)
  "Generate a tag index page for PROJECT."
  (let* ((filename (concat (project-dir "src" "org") "tags.org"))
         ;; Get all publically listed files in this project.
         (files (seq-filter (lambda (entry) (plist-get entry :indexed))
                            (tw-get-all-files project)))
         ;; Convert to sorted alist of tag×article pairs.
         (all-tags (sort (tw-get-all-file-tags files)
                         (lambda (a b) (string< (car a) (car b))))))
    (with-temp-file filename
      (insert (concat
               "#+TITLE: Tags\n"
               ;; Don't show author and publish date.
               "#+AUTHOR: \n"
               ;; Don't list in public indices.
               "#+FILETAGS: :page:\n\n"
               ;; Include table of contents.
               "#+TOC: headlines:1\n\n"
               ;; Then produce headings for each tag.
               (org-element-interpret-data
                   (tw-article-entry-headlines all-tags)))))
    ;; Return the filename of the created file. I don't
    ;; remember why. Maybe it's not necessary.
    filename))

First we filter out the articles that should be indexed from a list of all files
in the project. We pass this through the tw-get-all-file-tags function, which
produces an association list, which is like a dictionary in Emacs
Lisp. Each entry in the association list is a tag paired with a list of articles
that have that tag. That list is sorted alphabetically on the tag name, and then
it gets converted into an Org document that can be exported.

Note the ugly appearing again! We are converting a data structure to an
org-element tree, but then we convert that org-element tree into a string and
insert it into a string also representing an Org document. The right thing to do
would probably have been to construct the entire document as an org-element
tree, and then maybe export this tree without creating a temporary file in
between? But I have hacked this together with limited knowledge and now I’m
unwilling to spend time on it.

The magic that broke in this case was inside tw-get-all-file-tags which is
short:

(defun tw-get-all-file-tags (files)
  "Get an alist of all tags for FILES, as symbols."
  (tw-invert-alist
   (mapcar (lambda (file) (cons file (plist-get file :tags))) files)))

This creates an association list of file × tags pairs by mapping cons over the
files. Then tw-invert-alist takes that association list and flips it, to
become an association list of tag × files instead. This last function is what
used to be explicitly recursive and blew the stack, but now it’s fixed.

(defun tw-invert-alist (alist)
  "Invert ALIST, turning key-values into value-keys."
  (let ((inverted nil))
    ;; For each pair of key×values in alist …
    (dolist (key-values alist inverted)
      (let ((key (car key-values)))
        ;; … loop through all values …
        (dolist (value (cdr key-values))
          ;; … and store the key under the value
          ;; in the inverted list. If the value exists,
          ;; store the key in its list, otherwise
          ;; add the value and store a singleton list.
          (if (alist-get value inverted)
              (push key (alist-get value inverted))
            (push (cons value (list key)) inverted)))))))
In this version it builds the inverted association list iteratively instead.

blocks.text: On September 15, 1998, Diamond Multimedia introduced an MP3 player, the Diamond Rio PMP300. It wasn’t the first MP3 player, but it made the MP3 player mainstream. I had one. It wasn’t exactly great, but I understand why the RIAA was afraid of it. That’s one of the main reasons I spent $200 to get one. I got mine so early the RIAA hadn’t been able to sue Diamond Multimedia yet.
Rio PMP300: dreaming in digital (or at least playing)
In the 1980s, the Sony Walkman had been ubiquitous. It was a small, portable cassette player that clipped onto your belt and allowed you to take music anywhere. Everyone had one, or an imitator.

The Rio PMP300 showed what the new century’s version of the Walkman was going to look like. Plug it into your computer, load it up with MP3 files, and take your music with you. Only now it was solid state. No tapes to wear out or lose. It was a fully digital experience.

Diamond Multimedia wasn’t a familiar name in the consumer electronics space. They were a leading maker of PC components like video cards, so designing an MP3 player wasn’t much of a stretch for them. The Diamond Rio PMP300 gave them name recognition outside the realm of PC hardware enthusiasts.
How the RIAA’s lawsuit backfired
On October 8, 1998, three weeks and two days after its release, the Recording Industry Association of America asked for a restraining order to block the sale of the Rio PMP300.

The RIAA was afraid of it because it was dangerously mainstream. Diamond was a respected manufacturer of video cards and other computer accessories. It had relationships with national retailers like CompUSA, Best Buy, and Circuit City. And the PMP300 was absolutely a product those stores would be willing to carry. The first MP3 player on the market was an obscure device manufactured by Samsung, but carrying a brand with no name recognition, and you had to order it. The music press talked about it, but the computer media ignored it, and so did the mainstream media. The computer media talked about the Diamond Rio. And after the RIAA sued to block its sale, the mainstream media covered it.

That made the lawsuit backfire, because Diamond won. Their device didn’t facilitate piracy. It didn’t stop you from loading pirated MP3s on it, but owning one didn’t make the actual piracy of the files any harder or easier. It wasn’t Napster. That’s why the RIAA prevailed against Napster and even against MP3.com but not against Diamond.

I think the RIAA would have been better off if they had ignored the device. Because all they accomplished was calling a lot more attention to it. Suddenly, people who had no idea what an MP3 was suddenly knew that digital music existed, and that a device sold in consumer electronics stores would play those files. But we are talking the same organization that sued a 12-year-old here, so of course they’d sue Diamond Multimedia.

The legal tactics brought the MP3 mainstream sooner than it would have otherwise. Because the Diamond Rio in and of itself didn’t do a lot to mainstream the MP3. But the publicity from the lawsuit did. It wasn’t exactly free advertising, but it was more effective than any advertising Diamond could have done on its own.
After all these legal fights, it astonishes me that when the last MP3-related patent expired, it seemed like nobody really noticed.
Weaknesses of the Diamond Rio PMP300

The Diamond Rio PMP300 plugged into your PC parallel port. USB wasn’t something everyone had yet, and Windows 95 had either no support at all for it, or very poor support, depending on which version you happened to own. Windows 98 had better USB support, but in 1998, USB was definitely the connection of the future, not the present.

The parallel port was the best existing choice to plug your Diamond Rio in. Problem was, it was a crowded place. It was intended for printers. But if you had a scanner or a Zip drive, those wanted to plug into the parallel port as well. Chaining two devices off the parallel port usually worked. Chaining three was asking for trouble.
The Music Match software it came with to transfer files worked, but it wasn’t exactly elegant. I was able to figure it out, and I don’t recall it ever giving me trouble, but I was an IT professional.

On top of all that, it had very limited capacity. It had 32 MB of storage, enough to hold 30 minutes of music at 128 kbit/s. I re-encoded my MP3s at 64 kbit/s so I could carry an hour of music with me.
It wasn’t something I’d recommend to everyone. I had some friends who could totally figure it out. Other friends would have just gotten frustrated with it.
My experience with a Diamond Rio PMP300

It was the absolute epitome of a minimum viable product. At first I liked being able to load my selection of MP3s on it and rotate them as I got tired of one song and wanted to bring another one in. But eventually I got tired of that process, especially the part of needing to re-encode the music at a lower bitrate. In an era of 400 MHz CPUs being mainstream, the re-encoding process took some time.
I ended up loading it up with some all-time favorites that I wasn’t likely to get tired of, and using it to supplement the radio. If there was nothing decent on the radio, I fired up the Rio.

And then, one day, I brought it in from the car for the last time. I had no idea that was the last time. But I brought it in, and set it down on my desk so it would be ready when I wanted to load some different songs on it. And then I never got around to it. Eventually, instead of plugging it into my computer, I picked it up off my desk and put it in the drawer.

And I think that’s why it sold 200,000 units and quickly fell by the wayside. It was fine for an early adopter type, but the general public needed something a little more refined. Eventually even I wanted something a little more refined. I was happy with SanDisk’s players but of course the Apple iPod was the device that became the market leader.

My neglected Rio PMP300 sat in that desk for 10, maybe even 15 years. I moved from my apartment to my house, put the desk in the den, then later we moved the desk into the basement. Eventually my wife decided she wanted to use the desk, including the storage, so she cleared out the stuff that was in the drawers. Among the things she found were my Diamond Rio, my Swatch watch, and my Walkman knock off. Kind of a strange mix to wind up in the same drawer together.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

articles.title: There is no epidemic of loneliness, but there is an epidemic of scurvy
articles.titleZh: There is no epidemic of loneliness, but there is an epidemic of scurvy
articles.summary: There is no epidemic of loneliness, but there is an epidemic of scurvy

blocks.text: We’re living through an epidemic of loneliness and everybody knows it, except for one small group: people who have actually looked at the data.

Much of what appears to be a loneliness epidemic is, in fact, a well-intentioned misunderstanding. However, there is a real epidemic out there—one that is far stranger and more sinister. I’ll get to its causes and cures in a moment, but first:

When people think they’re documenting a concerning trend, they often get a little loosey-goosey with the facts. I don’t think anyone does this on purpose—no one is getting rich selling anti-loneliness pills (yet). But it means that claims about the loneliness epidemic are often tainted by two statistical sins that tend to go undetected.

First, someone will present one actual data point showing how many people feel lonely today, they’ll imply a data point from the past where people were less lonely, and then they’ll conclude, based on the trendline that they just made up, that something very bad has happened. For example, in this paper, researchers find that 76% of adults in California and 78% of adults in the Chinese province of Anhui are lonely, and then they ask why this “unprecedented worldwide rise in loneliness” has occurred. But we only know how these folks are feeling today—we have no idea what they would have said if we asked them yesterday, or a year ago, or ten years ago. It’s possible they’ve always been this lonely.1
The second bit of malfeasance is concluding that you’ve discovered a trend in loneliness when you’ve simply divided up the results by age, like this:
When you see a graph like that, it’s almost impossible not to rush to conclusions—these poor young people, sucked away from their friends by the black holes of YouTube and Instagram!

The faulty assumption here is that older people have never been lonely and that younger people will remain lonely forever. We don’t know if this is an age effect (maybe every generation grows out of its youthful loneliness) or a cohort effect (maybe kids these days, unlike their parents and grandparents, are doomed to lifetimes of loneliness). One way to separate these effects is to compare today’s kids to yesterday’s kids. And when you do that, you see declines, not increases:

More recent data suggests that teenage loneliness might have ticked back up to where it was in the 1980s, and the evidence here is mixed overall, depending on which data sets and cohorts you look at. We don’t yet have enough data to be sure which way the effects go on average, but we do have enough to be sure that those effects are neither large nor universal.
That doesn’t mean everything is fine. There is, in fact, another epidemic lurking next door...

Although the data does not show that people are more lonely, it does show that people are more alone. (Derek Thompson has made this point particularly well.) In the US, time spent with friends on the weekends has fallen by half in the past 20 years. According to the American Time Use Survey, pals are out and solitude is in:
This is mainly a recession in hanging out—most of the increase in alone time has come from people spending less time with folks outside their households2:

That 2022 time point could be a pandemic hangover, but time spent with non-household members was already dropping long before covid appeared. Indeed, from 1998 to 2018, people who live by themselves started spending much more time alone overall:
We’ve got a puzzle here. People are more alone than ever, but they’re not feeling much lonelier than they used to. So maybe all this extra solitude is...fine?

No, it’s not fine. Isolated people are more likely to get depressed, suffer a heart attack or a stroke, develop dementia, and catch a cold; they straight-up die sooner. (The “loneliness is as bad as smoking 15 cigarettes a day” meme is a bit dubious, but it’s also not crazy.) Those findings all come from correlational studies, but when you inflict isolation on someone instead, you quickly see some massive and concerning effects. Prisoners in solitary confinement often sink into a stupor, their thoughts become obsessive and delusional, and they get agitated and irritable. (I’ve heard many people complain of similar but milder things happening to their elderly parents who live alone.)

Here’s one extreme case that’s instructive: when a Spanish woman went into a cave alone for 500 days, to both set a record and prove a point, she turned loopy. She ended up flirting with her GoPro cameras, hallucinating the sound of shamans beating drums, and accusing her electrical equipment of poisoning her with sound waves. “There is no past, there is no future,” she later told a reporter. “Everything is present, everything is a while ago, and it’s all brutal and strange.”

Remember 2017, when everybody was making slime at home? Remember how the coolest slimes were the ones that are liquid when undisturbed, but turn solid when you squeeze or poke them? The human mind is kind of like that slime: it only has shape when prodded and pushed by the presence of other people. When left to its own devices, it turns to ooze. And that sticky, shapeless substance provides the perfect Petri dish for all of our current pathologies. The penchant for voting for extremists, the hyperfixation on gambling away your life savings on sports and crypto, the dream of perpetual gooning—these are the disordered desires of a mind that’s been liquified by solitude.

Too much alone time is clearly bad for us, but it doesn’t seem to bother us as much as it should. So the real mystery of the loneliness epidemic is: where is it? Why are we all sitting alone in our houses and slowly melting into puddles of slime, like the “this is fine” meme dog, but without the fire?
To answer that question, we need to understand another modern malady. Namely, scurvy.

If you don’t get enough vitamin C, you’ll start to feel tired and weak, your joints will hurt, your legs will swell, you’ll get spots on your skin, your teeth with fall out, you’ll feel grumpy all the time (understandably), and eventually, you’ll die. All of this can be prevented with a few tablespoons of lemon juice, but people suffering from scurvy do not develop a hankering for citrus. They will suffer and wither and collapse and never even ask for a grapefruit.

So not only are we unable to synthesize vitamin C ourselves—making us one of the few unlucky mammals who can’t—we are also apparently unable to desire vitamin C. This seems like a rather odd design flaw. If evolution didn’t endow us with a vitamin C dispenser, why couldn’t it at least endow us with a vitamin C detector and desire-er?
It’s easier to make sense of this when you think in terms of cybernetic psychology. I’ve written about this theory before (review here, expansion here), but here’s a quick recap:

Imagine the mind as a big stack of thermostats. In addition to regulating temperature, these thermostats try to keep all sorts of mission-critical variables at the correct levels—we’ve got a food-stat to make sure we don’t starve, a sleep-stat to make sure we get enough rest, a pain-stat to protect the body from damage, and so on.

Whenever one of these control systems—the general term for various -stats—detects that its target variable is out of whack, it tries to restore balance. When you haven’t eaten enough, for example, the food-stat starts sending you messages like “burritos sure are yummy” until you finally put food in your mouth. And once you’re full, the food-stat tries to stop you from bursting your stomach by sending you messages like “NEVER MIND BURRITOS ARE GROSS”.3

Our control systems have been good enough to keep us alive for several hundred thousand years. But they can go haywire when we subject them to modern environments for which they did not evolve, and that’s exactly what happens in the case of scurvy.

We don’t know exactly how our food-stat functions, but there’s a good chance it contains subsystems that look out for particular macronutrients: a carb-stat, perhaps, or a protein-stat, sugar-stat, salt-stat, and so on. Whatever those subsystems are, they’re enough to make us eat an omnivorous diet that provides sufficient vitamin C, which happens to appear in lots of different foods, like chickpeas, potatoes, cauliflower, and polar bear meat (yes, really).

That’s why scurvy doesn’t seem to have been a big problem for our ancestors. Although there are a few ancient accounts of sicknesses that sound kind of like scurvy, and there were unmistakable cases during military campaigns when the food situation turned dire, scurvy didn’t really hit the scene until the 1500s, when we figured out how to build boats big and tough enough to spend months at sea, with nary a glass of MinuteMaid in sight.4
You can see where I’m going with this: we are not living through an epidemic of loneliness. We are living through an epidemic of social scurvy.

Social deprivation looks a lot like vitamin C deprivation. In both cases, humans can lack an essential input without realizing it. In both cases, they can suffer for its absence without desiring its presence. And in both cases, this is probably because we evolved in an environment where we never needed that desire.

Of course, humans don’t completely lack the capacity to desire companionship the way we lack the capacity to desire vitamin C. We do get lonely; we just don’t get lonely enough. Compared to, say, our food-stats, our social-stats are rather anemic. When people starve, they’ll become obsessed with food; they’ll fantasize about opening restaurants and going hog wild at an all-you-can-eat buffet, and these desires will only increase until the person either eats or dies. For example, in this paper, researchers find that 76% of adults in California and 78% of adults in the Chinese province of Anhui are lonely, and then they ask why this “unprecedented worldwide rise in loneliness” has occurred. But we only know how these folks are feeling today—we have no idea what they would have said if we asked them yesterday, or a year ago, or ten years ago. It’s possible they’ve always been this lonely.1
The second bit of malfeasance is concluding that you’ve discovered a trend in loneliness when you’ve simply divided up the results by age, like this:
When you see a graph like that, it’s almost impossible not to rush to conclusions—these poor young people, sucked away from their friends by the black holes of YouTube and Instagram!

The faulty assumption here is that older people have never been lonely and that younger people will remain lonely forever. One way to separate these effects is to compare today’s kids to yesterday’s kids. And when you do that, you see declines, not increases:

More recent data suggests that teenage loneliness might have ticked back up to where it was in the 1980s, and the evidence here is mixed overall, depending on which data sets and cohorts you look at. That doesn’t mean everything is fine. There is, in fact, another epidemic lurking next door...

This is mainly a recession in hanging out—most of the increase in alone time has come from people spending less time with folks outside their households2:

That 2022 time point could be a pandemic hangover, but time spent with non-household members was already dropping long before covid appeared. Indeed, from 1998 to 2018, people who live by themselves started spending much more time alone overall:
We’ve got a puzzle here. People are more alone than ever, but they’re not feeling much lonelier than they used to. So maybe all this extra solitude is...fine?

I suppose because the things that make you crazy are the only things you’ll ever truly love. We evolved to tangle with each other, and we shrivel up and die if we don’t. Hell is other people? No way man. Hell is when your teeth fall out because nobody was there to remind you to eat an orange.

Once people have invented a concerning trend, they often feel free to invent its causes as well. For instance, this Weill Cornell page on the loneliness epidemic claims that people feel more lonely today because they’re more likely to move to new places—for college, retirement, etc. But this is untrue. As I wrote in a previous post, people are less likely to move today than they were in past decades.

This is only measuring the proportion of time that people could conceivably choose to spend with someone else. So it doesn’t include time spent sleeping, obviously, but it also doesn’t include time spent working. The author says the American Time Use Survey didn’t start asking people about time spent with others at work until 2010 anyway, and regardless, there were apparently no change in time spent alone at work between 2010 and 2019. So the increase in aloneness from 2003 to 2019 really does seem to be a matter of people choosing to be alone, or at the very least, being put in a state of solitude and not choosing to get themselves out of it.

The cybernetic model of psychology says that we get hits of happiness for re-aligning our control systems, and the bigger the correction, the greater the pleasure. That may be why asphyxiation is so often preceded by the word “erotic”, but I leave this as a matter for future research.

Here’s another example. All humans have an air-stat that causes them to freak out if they can’t breathe. The air-stat is one of the strongest control systems around—if someone’s squeezing your throat or you’ve been underwater for too long, every neuron you’ve got will be trying to figure out how to get a gulp of air. But it turns out that the air-stat is much more sensitive to the amount of carbon dioxide in the lungs than it is to the amount of oxygen. Historically, this was a fine proxy—if you’re not clearing your CO2, then something is clearly going wrong.

Recently, however, humans have invented ways to fiddle with the mix of gases around us, allowing us to adjust the level of oxygen without affecting the level of carbon dioxide. For instance, processing plants use liquid nitrogen to flash-freeze meat, and if that nitrogen leaks out, it’ll turn into gas that can displace the oxygen in the room. Because we are not as  sensitive to insufficient oxygen levels or to excess nitrogen levels—the atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen anyway—if you find yourself in this situation, you might become disoriented, fall unconscious, asphyxiate, and die, all without your air-stat sounding the alarm. That’s what happened in Georgia in 2021: six workers died at a poultry processing plant when a freezer malfunctioned and started spewing nitrogen gas. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration requires workplaces like these to deploy oxygen detectors precisely because humans do not come with those detectors preinstalled.

I’m familiar with this because a similar accident happened right outside my town shortly before I was born. A farmer entered a manure pit to try to clear a clog, but the methane fumes were so strong that he collapsed from a lack of oxygen. His brother came to rescue him and also collapsed. Sadly, both died. My parents would tell me this story whenever we drove past the farm, and it’s stuck with me ever since.
You might wonder: isn’t this just a matter of introversion vs. extraversion? Is the problem just that everyone needs to be a bit more extraverted?

This is a reasonable hypothesis, but it mixes up two distinct concepts. In cybernetic psychology, people’s thermostats differ not only in their set points—the target level that each control system is trying to maintain—but also in their sensitivities, which is how quickly and vigorously those systems will fight to restore balance when things go out of whack. A big beefy dude needs to eat more food to stay alive than a petite old lady does (different set points), but they could feel equally hungry when they don’t get their respective amounts of necessary nutrition (same sensitivities). If you turn down the sensitivities on their food-stats, both of them could end up equally malnourished, even if the beefy guy is eating more than the old lady.

The same thing could happen socially. Extraverts may need more social “nutrition” than introverts do—that’s the difference in set points. But if their control systems aren’t sensitive enough—that is, if they don’t respond strongly enough when they fail to reach their set point—both of them could end up socially malnourished, even if the extravert is spending more time with other people overall.

This study probably overestimated the increase in social craving simply by reminding participants that there was something to crave. And we have no idea if people would have acted on their cravings if they had the chance. Lots of people have to be coaxed into attending a party, but very few people have to be coaxed into eating dinner. In fact, millions of people will pay for GLP-1 drugs that they hope will help them resist eating dinner.

Why would our water-intake control systems leave us slightly high and dry? I have a few guesses:
Our evolutionary ancestors did not have constant and easy access to safe drinking water, so they needed to be able to endure some amount of dehydration without their hydro-stats freaking out.

Prehistoric foods probably contained more water than modern foods do (not a lot of crackers and Cheerios in the hunter-gatherer diet). So the food-stat was shouldering some of the hydro-stat’s burden.
Ancient humans consumed much less salt than we do today; their hydro-stats never had to contend with a tube of Pringles.
